text: Lie [AS. leogan ]: Ger. Lüge ; Fr. mensonge ; Ital. menzogna . Any intentional deception of another by positive misrepresentation. Cf. EQUIVOCATION. The essence of the lie rests in the intention to deceive; yet the means of the deception, by positive misrepresentation -- as contrasted with either negative suggestion ( suggestio falsi ) or omission of truth ( suppresio veri ) -- seems, though casuistical, to be well established. The following example from Macaulay ( Hist . of England , chap. ix) illustrates this 'distinction without a difference.' Bishop Compton, who had invited William of Orange to invade England in 1688, is asked by King James if there is any truth in the statement in William's manifesto that some spiritual peers had invited him; he replies: Sir, I am quite confident that there is no one of my brethren who is not as guiltless as myself in this matter.' Macaulay remarks: 'The equivocation was ingenious; but whether the difference between the sin of such an equivocation and the sin of a lie be worth any expense of ingenuity may perhaps be doubted.' The question of the ethical justification of a lie is also quite apart; whether right or not, a lie is a lie 'for a' that.' See VERACITY, and cf. CASUISTRY. ( J.M.B. - H.S. )
